title: Mostar Records the Scope of Croat Territorial Claims
sources: ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T), 29 May 2013
Balkan Battlegrounds, Vol. II (CIA, 2002), Central Bosnia operative-zone chronology
content:
In the summer of 1993 the HZ HB controlled its widest territorial footprint: the Mostar west bank consolidated after the May rupture with the ARBiH, the Herzegovina core around Posušje, Grude, Ljubuški, Čitluk, Široki Brijeg, and Tomislavgrad, the central-Bosnian pockets of the Vitez-Busovača-Kiseljak triangle plus the Žepče exclave, and a chain of checkpoints sustaining the Tuđman-Šušak airbridge from Croatia.

Mate Boban faced a foundational scope decision. The HZ HB had been founded on 18 November 1991 and upgraded to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on 28 August 1993, but the territorial ambition behind those declarations was never fixed. The Prlić judgment documents a spectrum running from a pragmatic consolidation of the defensible Herzegovina core, through the maximalist claim to all territory the HVO could hold, to the most expansive vision: a partition of Bosnia with the RS that would carve a Greater Croatia and a Greater Serbia from the corpse of the republic.

The Tuđman presidential transcripts admitted at Prlić show Zagreb weighing exactly this scope question, with the central-Bosnian pockets — militarily exposed and logistically dependent on the airbridge — as the marginal claim that determined whether Herceg-Bosna over-reached. Historically the HVO pursued the pragmatic maximum until the ARBiH counter-offensive of autumn 1993 and the Washington Agreement forced consolidation.

The scope recorded here conditions how far the Croat-Bosniak war ran and on what terms it could be ended.
